title: Florida JEAC Opinion 2026-01
subject: A judge who previously prosecuted a defendant as assistant state attorney may provide a response to a request from the Florida Commission on Offender Review regarding the defendant’s clemency review, in compliance with Florida Statutes. However, the judge may not provide unsolicited input to the Florida Commission on Offender Review regarding the clemency review, as such input is not contemplated by statute and therefore does not carry the same statutory protection.
text:
ISSUE
1. May a judge provide a response to a request directly from the Florida Commission on Offender Review regarding a clemency review?
ANSWER: Yes.
2. May a Judge provide unsolicited input to the Florida Commission on Offender Review regarding a clemency review?
ANSWER: No.

FACTS
The inquiring judge previously served as an assistant state attorney and prosecuted a defendant who is currently seeking an executive clemency review of his death sentence. Pursuant to Chapter 940, Florida Statutes (2025), the approved form for executive clemency applications may require notice to the judge who presided over the conviction and the prosecuting attorney of the court in which the applicant was convicted. The inquiring judge is aware that a clemency review is currently being conducted as to this defendant. Although the inquiring judge has not yet received an inquiry from the Florida Commission on Offender Review, they seek guidance on whether they can provide input if formally contacted. Additionally, they seek guidance on whether they can provide input in the absence of a direct request from the Florida Commission on Offender Review.

DISCUSSION
Canon 1 of the Code of Judicial Conduct is entitled, “A Judge Shall Perform the Duties of Judicial Office Impartially and Diligently” and requires in subsection B(9) in part that a “judge shall not, while a proceeding is pending or impending in any court, make any public comment that might reasonably be expected to affect its outcome or impair its fairness or make any nonpublic comment that might substantially interfere with a fair trial or hearing.” However, section C(1) states a “judge shall diligently discharge the judge's administrative responsibilities without bias or prejudice and maintain professional competence in judicial administration, and should cooperate with other judges and court officials in the administration of court business.”
Florida Statutes Chapter 940, Executive Clemency, provides that any applicant seeking review of a sentence under this Chapter may send a copy of their application to “the judge and prosecuting attorney of the court in which the applicant was convicted, notifying them of the applicant's intent to apply for executive clemency.” See §940.03, Fla. Stat. (2025). Similarly, Chapter 947, addressing parole and conditional release, requires as part of the review for conditional release that notice be sent to the sentencing judge, the Chief Judge or a circuit judge selected by the Chief Judge for a response. See §947.16(4)(c), Fla. Stat. (2025).
In JEAC Opinion 2002-04, the committee reviewed a similar request under the guidance of Canon 2. Canon 2 of the Code of Judicial Conduct is entitled "A Judge Shall Avoid Impropriety And the Appearance of Impropriety in All of the Judge's Activities." Canon 2A states, a “judge shall respect and comply with the law and shall act at all times in a manner that promotes public confidence in the integrity and impartiality of the judiciary.” In Op. 2002-04, this committee held, when contacted as a part of a Chapter 947 review, as the request was specifically contemplated by statute and Canon 2 requires that judges comply with the law, the inquiring judge was entitled to respond to the request.
We also addressed whether a judge could respond to a formal request from the Florida Parole Commission regarding a defendant’s attempt to obtain a waiver of the rules of executive clemency. In JEAC Opinion 2004-13, we answered affirmatively that a judge who recused themselves from a case could respond to the Florida Parole Commission's request for input on a defendant's request for waiver of rules of executive clemency.
As for the second issue which seeks guidance on whether the inquiring judge may provide unsolicited input, the committee answers in the negative as that would violate Canon 1 (B)(9) by making a comment that “might reasonably be expected to affect … [the] outcome or impair its fairness or make any nonpublic comment that might substantially interfere with a fair trial or hearing.” The previously cited opinions found guidance in the statute contemplating input from the sentencing judge, the Chief Judge or a circuit judge selected by the Chief Judge for a response. In the facts before this body today, we find the unsolicited input is not contemplated by statute and is therefore not cloaked in the same protection.

REFERENCES
Sections 940.03 and 947.16, Florida Statutes (2025).
Fla. Code Jud. Conduct, Canons 1B, 1C, and 2A.
Fla. JEAC Ops. 2004-13 and 2002-04.

SUBJECT
A judge who previously prosecuted a defendant as assistant state attorney may provide a response to a request from the Florida Commission on Offender Review regarding the defendant’s clemency review, in compliance with Florida Statutes. However, the judge may not provide unsolicited input to the Florida Commission on Offender Review regarding the clemency review, as such input is not contemplated by statute and therefore does not carry the same statutory protection.
